# sysutils_hostname (Resource)

Sets the host's static hostname in `/etc/hostname` and its kernel (transient) hostname, and optionally the pretty hostname in `/etc/machine-info` and a `127.0.1.1` line in `/etc/hosts`. Uses `hostnamectl` when systemd is PID 1 and the provider's `root_dir` is not set. Below `root_dir` only the files are written. There is one hostname per host, so there must be at most one `sysutils_hostname` per host (or per `root_dir`). On destroy the hostname stays as it is, unless `restore_on_destroy` is set.

## Example Usage

```terraform
# Name the host web1.example.com: /etc/hostname, the kernel hostname and,
# on systemd hosts, systemd-hostnamed all report it. The pretty hostname is
# what hostnamectl shows, and /etc/hosts gets
# "127.0.1.1 web1.example.com web1" so that the name resolves without DNS.
resource "sysutils_hostname" "this" {
  hostname           = "web1.example.com"
  pretty_hostname    = "Web server 1"
  manage_hosts_entry = true
}

# Put back the previous hostname when the resource is destroyed, for
# example on a shared test machine.
# resource "sysutils_hostname" "this" {
#   hostname           = "ci-runner-7"
#   restore_on_destroy = true
# }
```

<!-- schema generated by tfplugindocs -->
## Schema

### Required

- `hostname` (String) Static hostname, such as `"web1"` or `"web1.example.com"`, as defined by RFC 1123: labels of 1 to 63 letters, digits and hyphens that neither start nor end with a hyphen, separated by dots, at most 253 characters in all and without a trailing dot. The kernel holds at most 64 characters, so without `root_dir` the name must not be longer. Written to `/etc/hostname` and, without `root_dir`, set as the kernel hostname.

### Optional

- `manage_hosts_entry` (Boolean) Keep a line in `/etc/hosts` that maps `127.0.1.1` to `hostname` and, for a name with dots, its first label (`127.0.1.1 web1.example.com web1`), as Debian's installer writes it, so that the hostname resolves without DNS. A `127.0.1.1` line for the previous hostname is updated in place; other lines are kept. Turning it off leaves the line in place. Defaults to `false`.
- `pretty_hostname` (String) Free-form pretty hostname, such as `"Web server 1"`, stored as `PRETTY_HOSTNAME` in `/etc/machine-info` and shown by `hostnamectl`. Up to 255 bytes of UTF-8 without control characters or leading or trailing white space. Unset leaves the pretty hostname alone.
- `restore_on_destroy` (Boolean) Whether destroy puts back the hostnames that were set before the resource was created: `/etc/hostname`, the kernel hostname, the pretty hostname if `pretty_hostname` is set, and the `/etc/hosts` line if `manage_hosts_entry` is set. They are recorded in the resource's private state on create; after import there is nothing to restore, and destroy only warns. Defaults to `false`: destroy leaves the hostname as it is.

### Read-Only

- `id` (String) Always `"system"`.
- `transient_hostname` (String) The kernel hostname (`uname -n`). Equal to `hostname` after apply; a plan shows a change of this attribute when the kernel hostname was changed outside Terraform, for example by DHCP. Null when the provider's `root_dir` is set, since the kernel hostname is not managed then.

## Static, Transient and Pretty Hostname

A Linux host has three hostnames, as systemd names them:

- the **static hostname** in `/etc/hostname`, which the init system gives the kernel at boot (`hostname`);
- the **transient hostname**, the kernel's (`uname -n`), which is lost on reboot and which DHCP clients and container runtimes may change (`transient_hostname`);
- the **pretty hostname**, a free-form name such as `Web server 1` in `PRETTY_HOSTNAME=` of `/etc/machine-info`, which only `systemd-hostnamed` and its clients show (`pretty_hostname`).

`hostname` sets the first two to the same name. Names must follow RFC 1123 (labels of 1 to 63 letters, digits and hyphens, not starting or ending with a hyphen, at most 253 characters in all). The kernel holds at most 64 characters, so on the host a longer name is refused when planning; below `root_dir` it is fine.

## How the Hostname Is Set

- **With systemd as PID 1, `hostnamectl` installed, without `root_dir`**, and with the provider in the same UTS and mount namespaces as PID 1, `hostnamectl --static set-hostname` and `hostnamectl --pretty set-hostname` set the names, so that `systemd-hostnamed` sees the change as its own and tells its clients. If `hostnamectl` fails, for example because D-Bus is not running, the provider writes the files itself and reports the failure as a warning. The namespace check keeps a provider running in a container, or in a UTS namespace of its own, from renaming the host through `systemd-hostnamed`, which acts in PID 1's namespaces.
- **Otherwise**, `/etc/hostname` is replaced atomically with the name and a newline: the new content is written to a temporary file in `/etc`, which gets the old file's mode, owner, ACLs and SELinux label, and is renamed over it. A missing file is created with mode `0644`; a symlink at `/etc/hostname` is refused. The kernel hostname is set with `sethostname(2)`.
- **Below the provider's [`root_dir`](../index.md#root-directory)** only the files are written. The kernel hostname belongs to the running host, not to the tree, so it is left alone and `transient_hostname` is null.
- **The pretty hostname** is written to `/etc/machine-info` in the format `systemd-hostnamed` uses, quoted where needed (`PRETTY_HOSTNAME="Web server 1"`). Other keys, comments and blank lines are kept. Without `pretty_hostname`, the file is not touched.
- **With `manage_hosts_entry = true`**, `/etc/hosts` gets the line `127.0.1.1 <hostname> <first label>`, as Debian's installer writes it (`127.0.1.1 web1.example.com web1`, or `127.0.1.1 web1` for a single-label name), so that `hostname -f`, `sudo` and other programs resolve the hostname without DNS. A `127.0.1.1` line for the previous hostname, the one in `/etc/hostname` on create or the one last applied, is updated in place, keeping its spacing; other lines, including other `127.0.1.1` lines, are kept byte for byte. If another line maps the hostname to a different IPv4 address, the resolver may use that one, and the provider warns. The file is edited with the same code and the same lock as [`sysutils_hosts_entry`](./hosts_entry.md).
- Nothing is written if a name is already set, and edits of the three files are [serialised](../index.md#concurrency-and-locking) with other resources of the provider.

Running programs that have read the hostname, such as a shell prompt or a mail server, keep the old one until they are restarted.

## Drift Detection

On refresh, the static hostname is read from `/etc/hostname` (its first line that is neither blank nor a comment) and the kernel hostname from the kernel. They are compared separately, so the plan shows which one was changed outside Terraform:

- `hostname` changes when `/etc/hostname` holds another name or is missing;
- `transient_hostname` changes when only the kernel hostname differs, for example after a DHCP client set it;
- `pretty_hostname`, if set, changes when `PRETTY_HOSTNAME` in `/etc/machine-info` differs or is missing;
- `manage_hosts_entry`, if `true`, shows as changing from `false` when the `127.0.1.1` line for the hostname is missing, duplicated or has other names.

Applying the plan sets only what differs.

## Destroy and `restore_on_destroy`

By default destroy leaves the hostname, the pretty hostname and the `/etc/hosts` line as they are: there is no sensible hostname to fall back to.

With `restore_on_destroy = true`, destroy puts back what was there when the resource was created. On create, before changing anything, the provider records the content of `/etc/hostname` (or that it was missing), the kernel hostname, the pretty hostname and whether `/etc/machine-info` existed, and the `127.0.1.1` line for the old hostname in the resource's private state, which Terraform stores with the state but does not show. Destroy restores `/etc/hostname` exactly and sets the recorded kernel hostname; the pretty hostname if `pretty_hostname` is set (removing a `/etc/machine-info` that did not exist, unless something else has been added to it); and, if `manage_hosts_entry` is set, the recorded `127.0.1.1` line in place of the managed one, or removes the managed line if there was none. Where `hostnamectl` is used for applying, it sets the recorded static and pretty hostnames first.

An imported resource has no recorded previous hostname; with `restore_on_destroy = true`, its destroy leaves the hostname in place and warns.

## Import

There is one hostname per host, so the import ID is always `system`:

```shell
# There is one hostname per host, so the import ID is always "system".
terraform import sysutils_hostname.this system
```

Import reads the static hostname from `/etc/hostname` and fails if it holds none. `pretty_hostname` is not read on import, and `manage_hosts_entry` and `restore_on_destroy` are `false`; set them in the configuration and apply.

## Caveats

- There is one hostname per host, or per `root_dir`. Two `sysutils_hostname` resources for the same host fight over it, and so do a `sysutils_hostname` and a [`sysutils_file`](./file.md) managing `/etc/hostname`, or a [`sysutils_hosts_entry`](./hosts_entry.md) for `127.0.1.1` with the same name.
- Cloud-init resets the hostname on every boot unless `preserve_hostname: true` is set in its configuration, and some DHCP clients set the kernel hostname from the lease. The next plan then shows the drift.
- Some distributions keep the hostname elsewhere too, such as `HOSTNAME=` in `/etc/sysconfig/network` on old RHEL releases or `/etc/conf.d/hostname` on OpenRC-based Gentoo; those files are not changed. Alpine's OpenRC `hostname` service reads `/etc/hostname`.
- Setting the kernel hostname needs root (`CAP_SYS_ADMIN`). In a container it changes only the container's UTS namespace.
- The resource only works on Linux.
